315.history: The hill of the first kingdom. Ailean Mòr came to it from the grove in the first summer with eleven of his kin, sat under its lip through the first winter hearing the households of the valleys, and set the flint-pit to making spearheads for anyone who asked. The bank was pegged out in the snow of the second spring and raised in the ninth year, with antler picks and flint scrapers; Gormshuil kept its gate, and after her, Rìghrean na Cloiche held it for the king, twelve in all, from Dòmhnall Clachach to Catrìona Mhòr. Sìleas Bhàn cut grain-pits into the bank and opened them by the count of mouths; Tormod Liath paced out the second bank and doubled the ground within it to near a hundred houses. Here the sharing before the storms began, here Calum Ciar asked for the slab's lot, and here Catrìona's cord was knotted to nine hundred hearths. In the last years the valley below the hill filled with the tents of the king's kin, each line with its own fire and its own steward, waiting on shares the king would not give.
315.known_for: the king's hill, the bank and the store within it

209.history: The grey oak grove where the six pots of na Seachd Guail were set under the oldest trees and Ailean kept his seven nights, fasting, until Coimhdeach na Fine named him king. Coinneach, his brother, camped beyond the ring of oaks and could not cross it; he found his brother warm at dawn with the frost standing off him in a bare ring. For more than two thousand years no household built there, the grove being held the king's and Coimhdeach na Fine's and no one's else. In the two thousand four hundred and seventieth year households of the near valleys came down into its shelter and marked the old oaks for their byres; Somhairle asked Fearchar mac Ailig's household to spare the three oldest trunks, because his father had once set pots beneath them, and they cut their beams from younger growth. The houses ringed the three oaks within a generation, and the place was called the ring under the oaks. In the later centuries the moor crept up on it from the north, and the oaks drew back into the sheltered hollows.
209.known_for: the vigil and the three oaks left standing

238.history: A red headland on the north-west coast where fishing households kept lines and hide boats long before the hill had a king. The king's word reached it late and lightly: it sent no spears to any quarrel of the valleys and was asked for none. In the hungry years, when the fishing failed along that whole coast and the graves at Baile chrom were laid two deep, Sìleas Bhàn's grain came up the shore to the headland in carts, and its households kept the custom of the store after, laying a season's fish by against the next bad year. Its boats went out further than most on that coast, and its people told the voyage of the first boats as their own. Its fishers cut the eight wind-names on the rock of the headland in the manner of Eilean fhada, a notch facing each way, and a boat that came home in the dark steered by the fire on the Baile chrom headland to the north once that fire was kept.
238.known_for: a headland of hide boats on the north-west coast

61.history: A fair hill of sheltered farms in the north-east, settled long before the grove and keeping its old ways through the whole of na Bliadhnachan Fada. The king's word reached it late and lightly, and it was never asked for spears. Its barley went down to Seann-Dhaoine' harbour at Seann Tarr while there were Seann-Dhaoine there to take it, and to the hill-folk who settled Seann Tarr after them. It sent its young to Cruinneachadh an Àtha from the time the gathering became yearly, and its ale went south with them.
61.known_for: barley, and the road to Seann Tarr

454.history: The oldest hearths of Na Glinn Àrda stand at Achadh dhìreach. In the nine hundred and second year three brothers clearing a strip for barley turned up a hearth laid true and never lit, and the valley left the strip unploughed and covered the hearth with peat until no living person remembered where it lay. Anna nic Coinnich was born two fields from it and kept the full hand all her life. In the thousand and sixty-sixth year Eanraig Ruadh, old and cold, burned a whole basket of an gual dathach in one night, and his house went up in a flame of a colour no one had a word for, with his wife Beathag and a grandchild within; the hearthstone split and ran with colour until the king knelt and laid his hand across it and it greyed. The king named the full hand a good custom and made no law of it. Eanraig's son kept the grey stone for his new hearth, and one of the four stone cups was ground here in Oighrig's years.
454.known_for: the unlit hearth and the basket burning

277.history: A rough ford on the drovers' road through Na Glinn Àrda, where the beasts were rested and watered. In a hearth of peat ash here the valleys say an gual dathach was first burned by a household outside Clann a' Chlachair, one sliver at a time. The custom of the full hand is told as beginning among the few households of this ford, after a sick child was warmed too generously, and from here it spread to every hearth of Na Glinn Àrda within a few years. In Oighrig's keeping a woman of Àth gharbh ground the first of the copies of the stone cup, measuring against Niocol Snaidhear's cup throughout, and she finished it quickest of the three. Coinneachadh nan Cupan was held at a nameless spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach, chosen because it lay equal walking from all four places. The drovers who rested there carried the custom of the full hand and the tidings of the cups the length of Na Glinn Àrda, and the ford's own households were among the first to sit a turn at the slab when the watch was drawn from every part of the hills.
277.known_for: the drovers' ford where the full hand began
